title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lianmin Chen, Junbin Qiu, Chenxing Wei, Yao Shu, Kun He
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliable application to reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results naturally lead to ZO-BOLT, which applies ZO optimization to BOLT's RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.

infographic.key_insight: Matching data across zeroth-order finite-difference evaluations cancels oracle noise, while mismatched on-policy evaluations amplify it as 1/μ².
infographic.engineering_relevance: ZO-BOLT offers a route to memory-efficient LLM post-training by applying zeroth-order optimization to an RLVR-aligned weighted-SFT objective.
method: Analyze gradient-estimation variance under matched versus mismatched evaluation data.
Derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants separating the two regimes.
Apply zeroth-order optimization to Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT).
infographic.evidence_signal: Perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched comparisons support the theory; tests across three model variants and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over pretrained baselines with near-inference memory use.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable implementation requires preserving data matching across paired evaluations; the abstract does not establish generalization beyond the tested models and math benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
authors: Jiaxin Xie, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, Wensheng Yu
abstract: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the formal verification capabilities of the Rocq proof assistant. It incorporates task classification, tool-assisted execution, verification feedback, and state-based task management to support the generation, refinement, and verification of formal proofs. Unlike an approach focused on a single mathematical theory, the agent is examined through case studies involving Morse--Kelley axiomatic set theory (MK), real numbers, propositional logic, and equivalences of the axiom of choice. These cases investigate its applicability across mathematical foundations and distinguish source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a unified operational framework for heterogeneous foundation-level tasks and clarify the gap between such a framework and a fully integrated mathematical foundation.

infographic.key_insight: MFF-Agent combines LLM reasoning with Rocq verification in a unified workflow for formalizing multiple areas of mathematical foundations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a reusable architecture for proof automation that combines tool execution, verification feedback, and explicit task-state management.
method: Classify formalization tasks and manage their execution state.
Use LLM reasoning and tools to generate and refine formal proofs.
Incorporate Rocq verification feedback into the workflow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Case studies cover Morse–Kelley set theory, real numbers, propositional logic, and axiom-of-choice equivalences, distinguishing source completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports feasibility rather than quantitative performance, and a unified workflow does not establish a fully integrated mathematical foundation.
infographic.paper_title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations

title: Embedding a de Rham Complex Structure into Eig-PIELM for Maxwell Eigenvalue Problems
authors: Hao Kang, Liang Li, Xing Li
abstract: The perfect electric conductor (PEC) boundary condition alone does not eliminate the gradient nullspace of the Maxwell curl-curl operator. Consequently, a boundary-only Maxwell implementation of Eig-PIELM, an eigenvalue extension of the physics-informed extreme learning machine (PIELM), may retain represented gradient modes in its reduced trial space, producing nonphysical, gradient-contaminated modes. We develop dR-Eig-PIELM, a finite-dimensional structure-preserving extension that retains the linear-coefficient, boundary-null-space, and one-shot multimode architecture of Eig-PIELM. It combines compatible tensor-product grad--curl trial spaces with a constrained null-space construction to restrict the sampled PEC space to the mass-orthogonal complement of the represented gradient image before the eigensolve. Symmetric weak-form Gram assembly yields a symmetric-definite reduced eigenproblem without an eigenvalue cutoff under the stated sampling and material-positivity assumptions. For rectangles and cuboids, we establish fixed-degree exactness at the PEC vector-field space and derive rank and dimension identities. Numerical experiments show that dR-Eig-PIELM excludes the spurious eigenmodes with significant gradient components observed in the boundary-only baseline. The method exhibits rapid convergence with increasing polynomial degree and competitive work--precision performance in the tested configurations. A covariantly mapped waveguide example illustrates the potential of dR-Eig-PIELM for integration into design optimization workflows through a constrained local geometry update driven by computed cutoff frequencies and their sensitivities. This work provides a mathematical and computational framework for separating represented gradient modes from physical Maxwell eigenmodes within Eig-PIELM and supports its use in waveguide spectral analysis and geometry design.

infographic.key_insight: dR-Eig-PIELM removes represented gradient modes before the Maxwell eigensolve, preventing a source of nonphysical modes that PEC boundary conditions alone cannot eliminate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports waveguide spectral analysis and geometry design using computed cutoff frequencies and their sensitivities.
method: Build compatible tensor-product grad–curl trial spaces.
Constrain the sampled PEC space to the mass-orthogonal complement of represented gradients.
Assemble symmetric weak-form Gram matrices for a one-shot multimode, symmetric-definite eigensolve.
infographic.evidence_signal: Rectangle and cuboid tests show exclusion of gradient-contaminated spurious modes, rapid polynomial-degree convergence, and competitive work–precision performance; a mapped waveguide example demonstrates a constrained local geometry update.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees depend on sampling and material-positivity assumptions, and fixed-degree exactness is established for rectangles and cuboids rather than general geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Embedding a de Rham Complex Structure into Eig-PIELM for Maxwell Eigenvalue Problems

title: What Drives the Zero-to-One Jump? Diagnosing and Steering Hard-Prompt Learning in RLVR
authors: Rui Zhu, Yumou Liu, Zhenzhe Zheng, Fan Wu
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has substantially improved mathematical reasoning, yet progress on hard prompts often stalls: a prompt can remain unsolved for many training steps before abruptly transitioning to solved--a discrete "zero-to-one" jump whose underlying dynamics and steerability remain poorly understood. We investigate two questions: what drives this transition, and can it be steered? Through event-based analysis measuring the time-to-first-positive (TTFP), we find that negative rollouts preceding successful transitions consistently retain higher early-stage generation entropy, distinguishing near-solvable failures from dead ends. This signal motivates NAPO (Negative-Augmented Policy Optimization), a method integrated with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) that ranks negatives in unsolved groups via an early-branching driver and assigns graded advantages, injecting informative gradients precisely where standard group-relative updates vanish. Under fixed rollout budgets, NAPO accelerates early solution discovery and improves Pass@256 by 10.0 points on AIME24 and 6.6 points on AIME2025, demonstrating that zero-to-one transitions are diagnosable and steerable through driver-guided negative learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/jameszhu-pixel-time/Z2O.

infographic.key_insight: Hard math prompts can jump from unsolved to solved, and higher early-generation entropy in failed rollouts signals failures closer to that transition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: NAPO turns otherwise uninformative all-failure rollout groups into training signals, improving hard-prompt learning under fixed rollout budgets.
method: Measure time-to-first-positive (TTFP) to analyze first-solution events.
Rank failed rollouts in unsolved groups using an early-branching driver.
Integrate graded negative advantages into GRPO where standard group-relative updates vanish.
infographic.evidence_signal: Under fixed rollout budgets, NAPO accelerates early solution discovery and improves Pass@256 by 10.0 points on AIME24 and 6.6 points on AIME2025.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether the entropy-based signal generalizes beyond the evaluated math settings.
infographic.paper_title: What Drives the Zero-to-One Jump? Diagnosing and Steering Hard-Prompt Learning in RLVR

title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
authors: Simon Matrenok, Nicolas Menet, Nicolas Flammarion, Andreas Krause
abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated-sampling objectives such as pass@k and max@k can reduce sharpening by shifting learning pressure toward harder prompts, and standard single-completion objectives can reproduce their optimal policies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KAPPO adapts existing policy optimizers to repeated-sampling objectives without otherwise changing training procedures, enabling control over behavioral coverage at lower sampling cost.
method: Derive closed-form optimal policies for KL-regularized pass@k and max@k.
Reproduce those optima using prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation.
Apply KAPPO after a one-time reference calibration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation report sharpening control and single-completion training that matches multi-completion @k optimizer performance at a fraction of the cost.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify calibration overhead or cost savings, so deployment-specific efficiency needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training

title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
authors: Xujun Che, Depeng Xu, Jian Xiang, Taufiqua Khan
abstract: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

infographic.key_insight: ProofPatch helps humans review whether Lean statements express their intent, then tracks when formalization changes require those judgments to be revisited.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It adds semantic change tracking and declaration pinning to protect reviewed formal specifications during human or LLM-driven edits.
method: Use kernel-checked probes to investigate unnecessary hypotheses or possible counterexamples.
Store review decisions with fingerprints of elaborated statements and their dependencies, rather than source text.
Revisit affected decisions after semantic changes and block patches that alter pinned declarations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 229 Mathlib revision pairs, ProofPatch flagged 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions for re-review; kernel evidence achieved 0.88–0.96 precision on 1,527 labeled statements, and no pinned-statement change passed in 344 LLM-agent runs.
infographic.watch_item: Kernel evidence supports human judgment but cannot establish that a formal statement captures its intended meaning; the change-tracking evaluation used synthetic review decisions.
infographic.paper_title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve

title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees
authors: Georgiy Malaniya, Anton Bolychev, Pavel Osinenko
abstract: Many control tasks require driving the system into a prescribed goal set and subsequently keeping it there. The considered setting assumes that a working controller is available that provably reaches and maintains the goal, albeit with suboptimal performance. This controller is referred to as the fallback policy. Conversely, although state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms can discover policies with impressive empirical performance, the neural networks at their core act as opaque black boxes learned through data-driven exploration and, as such, provide no theoretical mechanism to guarantee that the system will ever reach---and stay within---the prescribed goal set. This article presents CALF-Wrapper, a method that combines the fallback policy with a pretrained RL base policy and uses the critic estimate associated with the base policy to select between them during deployment. The theoretical analysis establishes that CALF-Wrapper inherits the goal-reaching property of the fallback policy under the stated assumptions and provides probability bounds for the settling time and the maximum distance from the goal set over a prescribed time interval. The experimental study evaluates CALF-Wrapper in four simulated control environments of different complexity. Comparisons include the base policy, fallback policy, and constrained reinforcement-learning methods formulated for the same objective. Sensitivity and ablation studies provide direct hyperparameter recommendations. The experiments show how CALF-Wrapper can provide effective task performance while attaining the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate. CALF-Wrapper requires no additional dynamics model, online learning, or constrained optimization during execution.

infographic.key_insight: CALF-Wrapper combines a pretrained RL policy with a proven fallback controller to inherit goal-reaching and goal-maintenance guarantees under stated assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables deployment of performance-oriented RL controllers without requiring an additional dynamics model, online learning, or constrained optimization during execution.
method: Start with a fallback policy that provably reaches and maintains the goal set.
Use the pretrained RL policy’s critic estimate to select between the RL and fallback policies.
Establish inherited goal-reaching guarantees and probability bounds on settling time and maximum distance from the goal.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation in four simulated control environments compares base, fallback, and constrained-RL policies, with sensitivity and ablation studies reporting effective performance and the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on the stated assumptions and a provably effective fallback policy; simulation success alone does not establish real-world reliability.
infographic.paper_title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees

title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition
authors: Andrea Violante, Nicola Rares Franco, Andrea Manzoni
abstract: Reduced-order models (ROMs) learned from trusted numerical simulations enable the real-time simulation of complex physical systems, making computationally prohibitive tasks-such as uncertainty quantification and optimal control-tractable. In particular, data-driven ROMs are opening the opportunity to learn from both numerical simulations and experimental data. However, integrating these sources of information is far from straightforward. Real-world measurements often involve multiple sources of uncertainty, including non-Gaussian noise, latent heterogeneities, unknown or hidden system parameters, and multiscale phenomena occurring below the resolution of the data. Consequently, real-world data are better described by parametrized stochastic partial differential equations, for which the development of effective ROMs remains relatively unexplored. In this work, we introduce POD-CNF, a data-driven generative ROM for efficient uncertainty quantification of parametrized high-dimensional systems. The approach combines projection-based model reduction and deep generative modeling. First, Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) is employed to obtain a low-dimensional representation of the solution manifold. A Conditional Normalizing Flow (CNF) is then trained to approximate the density of the reduced coefficients conditionally on the input parameters. This formulation allows the surrogate to capture complex, multimodal output distributions, going beyond standard regression-based ROMs and least-squares predictions. We assess the effectiveness of POD-CNF through numerical experiments, demonstrating its ability to accurately reproduce output distributions while substantially reducing computational costs. Finally, a proof-of-concept application illustrates how the generative paradigm facilitates integration into Bayesian inverse problems, highlighting promising directions for future research.

infographic.key_insight: POD-CNF combines proper orthogonal decomposition with conditional normalizing flows to learn parameter-dependent solution distributions for stochastic PDEs, rather than only point predictions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The generative reduced-order model enables efficient uncertainty quantification for high-dimensional physical systems and offers a route to Bayesian inverse modeling.
method: Compress solution snapshots into low-dimensional coefficients using proper orthogonal decomposition.
Train a conditional normalizing flow to model coefficient distributions given input parameters.
Sample reduced coefficients and reconstruct solution fields to represent complex, multimodal uncertainty.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report accurate reproduction of output distributions with substantially reduced computational costs, alongside a proof-of-concept Bayesian inverse application.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or speedup metrics, leaving performance across parameter regimes and rare events unclear.
infographic.paper_title: POD-CNF: reduced order modeling of parametrized stochastic PDEs via normalizing flows and proper orthogonal decomposition

title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems
authors: Jiale Lao, Immanuel Trummer
abstract: For over 50 years, the database community has developed a wide range of successful engines to answer two fundamental questions: how can database systems run faster, and how can we ensure their correctness? Experience with these engines shows that performance depends on hardware and workloads. As both change over time, we repeatedly redesign and rebuild database systems, a time-consuming and expensive process. Correctness remains another long-standing challenge: recent studies continue to uncover wrong-answer bugs even in mature database engines, despite years of development and testing. To address these, we present GenDB-V, a system that enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized to hardware and workloads for performance, and formally verified for correctness. GenDB-V supports specialized implementations of SQL templates and general-purpose engines that accept any query within a supported SQL subset. First, we develop SQLSpec to formalize SQL semantics and deterministically construct fixed, implementation-agnostic synthesis targets. Second, we enable joint synthesis of fast code and formal proofs through storage--execution co-optimization, performance-first exploration, and three-layer modular proofs that bridge low-level execution to SQLSpec semantics. Third, we verify the synthesized code and proofs against the fixed synthesis targets in an isolated pipeline, proving SQL correctness and program safety. We evaluate GenDB-V on TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR. For verified template implementations, GenDB-V achieves geometric-mean speedups of 22.0-61.3x over DuckDB and Umbra. For a verified general-purpose engine, GenDB-V also achieves speedups of 1.27-3.4x on TPC-H. GenDB-V also achieves better performance than a testing-based LLM synthesis method, while our audit and tests expose incorrect answers in that method's implementations for 16 of 28 templates.

infographic.key_insight: GenDB-V enables AI agents to synthesize database engines specialized for hardware and workloads, with formal guarantees of SQL correctness and program safety.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a path to faster database implementations without relying solely on costly manual optimization and testing for correctness.
method: Formalize SQL semantics with SQLSpec and construct fixed, implementation-independent synthesis targets.
Jointly synthesize fast code and modular proofs using storage–execution co-optimization and performance-first exploration.
Check generated code and proofs against the fixed targets in an isolated verification pipeline.
infographic.evidence_signal: On TPC-H and SEC-EDGAR, verified template implementations achieve 22.0–61.3× geometric-mean speedups over DuckDB and Umbra; a verified general-purpose engine achieves 1.27–3.4× speedups on TPC-H.
infographic.watch_item: Correctness guarantees are relative to SQLSpec and the supported SQL subset; the abstract does not establish coverage of full SQL or production-scale workloads.
infographic.paper_title: Stop Handcrafting Your Engine! GenDB-V: Towards AI-Generated and Formally Verified Database Systems

title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
authors: Nicola Farenga, Andrea Manzoni
abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

infographic.key_insight: Velocity Matching learns continuous-time dynamics without training-time rollouts, avoiding long-horizon objective degeneration and numerical-solver bias.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For nonlinear ODE and semi-discretized PDE models, it offers a way to learn accurate dynamics without repeatedly simulating and backpropagating through numerical solvers.
method: Use piecewise-linear trajectory interpolation and stochastic collocation to construct a simulation-free velocity objective.
Approximate velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step.
Link velocity errors to trajectory errors through stability estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on nonlinear ODEs and semi-discretized time-dependent PDEs report improved accuracy over trajectory-based objectives; the abstract provides no quantitative gains.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on temporal sampling resolution; the abstract does not establish robustness to noisy or sparsely sampled observations.
infographic.paper_title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities

title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction
authors: Faruk Alpay, Taylan Alpay
abstract: We develop nonreciprocal spherical attention as a mathematical framework for coarsening and compressed nearest-neighbor retrieval. For two shrinking acute blocks whose centers have zero skew pairing and whose total mass ratio is subexponential in inverse temperature, we prove $\lim_{β\to\infty}β^{-1}\log T_β=1-\cosφ$, without restricting particle-count growth. An explicit three-body flow has two rigorously separated metastable exponents. For finite compression, mass centering yields a sharp $O(r^2)$ attention-output error bound at fixed temperature, with an explicit spherical-normalization correction. We formulate skew query-side score calibration as a strictly convex moment problem and derive a unique normal equation, residual-based optimization certificates, and bounded low-rank projections. A norm-aware margin objective calibrates native squared-distance rankings. Experiments use semantic retrieval data, one million visual descriptors with three codebook seeds, and a ten-million-vector FAISS IVF-PQ index with recomputed exact cosine ground truth. On SIFT1M, skew margin calibration raises native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948; symmetric calibration reaches 0.8996. The ten-million-vector index reaches 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms per query in a four-thread batch benchmark, while validation selects no skew update. Exact streamed attention over ten million keys evaluates compressed memory on 1,024 held-out queries. Independent matrix solves, automatic differentiation, finite differences, interval arithmetic, full-flow tests, and nine Rocq-checked algebra lemmas support reproducibility. Directionality alone does not establish retrieval superiority.

infographic.key_insight: Nonreciprocal spherical attention yields a sharp coarsening-time exponent of 1 − cos φ under stated assumptions, alongside certified corrections for compressed retrieval scores.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Mass-centered compression provides O(r²) attention-output error at fixed temperature, while calibrated scores can improve compressed nearest-neighbor rankings.
method: Prove coarsening clocks for shrinking spherical blocks and separated metastable exponents in a three-body flow.
Derive compression-error bounds with an explicit spherical-normalization correction.
Fit skew score corrections through a strictly convex moment problem, with residual certificates and bounded low-rank projections.
infographic.evidence_signal: On SIFT1M, skew calibration improves native-L2 hit@10 from 0.8926 to 0.8948 versus 0.8996 for symmetric calibration; a 10-million-vector index achieves 0.8827 hit@10 at 0.1794 ms/query in a four-thread batch benchmark.
infographic.watch_item: Directionality does not guarantee retrieval gains: validation selected no skew update for the 10-million-vector index.
infographic.paper_title: Nonreciprocal Spherical Attention and Retrieval: Sharp Coarsening Clocks and Certified Score Correction

title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
authors: Zhipu Cui, Helin Gong, Shengfeng Zhu
abstract: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model that turns a natural-language problem description into a set of verified optimization results without manual solver-code development or debugging. The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localizes errors using independent sources of evidence, and completes constrained repairs automatically, thereby providing efficient end-to-end automation, autonomous execution, and verifiable results. We evaluated Agent4FreeFem on a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems. Every case passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.

infographic.key_insight: Agent4FreeFem turns natural-language topology optimization problems into verified results through LLM-driven execution and automated, constrained code repair.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets expert-intensive solver development and debugging that slow topology optimization workflows in aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering.
method: Preserve the original problem definition throughout the pipeline.
Localize errors using independent sources of evidence.
Automatically apply constrained repairs within stage-specific budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems, every case passed runtime verification and completed within each stage’s repair budget.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report benchmark size or verification criteria, so runtime success alone should not be equated with physical correctness or design optimality.
infographic.paper_title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
authors: Rileigh Bandy, Teresa Portone, Mohammad Khalil, Eric Crislip, Kyle Neal
abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

infographic.key_insight: Staged closure learning trades some accuracy for substantially fewer model evaluations and more robust optimization than embedded training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning unresolved dynamics offline can reduce training costs for simulation-based engineering workflows.
method: Compare embedded closure training with a two-stage data-assimilated approach.
Infer state and closure trajectories from observations, then train a closure model offline.
Evaluate both approaches on a synthetic SIQR epidemiological model with nonlinear, state-dependent quarantine.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the synthetic SIQR study, embedded training achieved the best average accuracy, while staged training preserved comparable qualitative behavior with moderately higher error and substantially fewer model evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The findings come from one synthetic exemplar; accuracy and efficiency gains may depend on the system and assimilated trajectory quality.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches

title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning
authors: Atsutomo Yara, Yoshikazu Terada
abstract: We consider nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation of the intensity function of a Poisson process, allowing the intensity to depend on observed covariates. Such models describe how event rates vary with external conditions, including conditions under which the intensity becomes arbitrarily small or vanishes. However, risk analysis based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence typically requires the true intensity to be bounded away from zero, a restrictive assumption in applications. We develop a unified approach that avoids this assumption and derive an oracle inequality for the covariate-averaged Hellinger distance between the true intensity and the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). As an application of the oracle inequality, we establish convergence rates for NPMLEs based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Our results show that, as in nonparametric regression, the ability of DNNs to capture underlying structure leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, DNN-based NPMLEs mitigate the curse of dimensionality when the true intensity has a compositional structure and automatically adapt to a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold structure of the event space. For intensity functions with a compositional structure, DNN-based NPMLEs achieve nearly minimax-optimal convergence rates without explicitly incorporating this structure into the network architecture. Simulations demonstrate that DNN-based estimators outperform kernel estimators in most settings, while manifold kernels remain competitive in some designs. Finally, we analyze stimulus-evoked neural spiking using data from the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels project. DNN-based NPMLEs provide better out-of-sample performance than a conditional kernel estimator, as evaluated by held-out log-likelihood.

infographic.key_insight: Deep-network Poisson intensity estimators admit Hellinger-risk guarantees even when true intensities vanish, with improved convergence rates under compositional or low-dimensional manifold structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports flexible event-rate modeling from observed covariates, including neural spiking applications where rates may approach zero.
method: Estimate covariate-dependent intensities using nonparametric maximum likelihood.
Derive an oracle inequality for covariate-averaged Hellinger distance without a positive lower bound on intensity.
Apply the bound to deep neural networks, obtaining nearly minimax-optimal rates for compositional intensities and adaptation to manifold structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations favor DNN estimators over kernels in most settings, and Allen Brain Observatory neural-spiking data show better held-out log-likelihood than a conditional kernel estimator.
infographic.watch_item: DNN estimators are not uniformly superior: manifold kernels remain competitive in some simulation designs.
infographic.paper_title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning

title: Can LLMs Reliably Evaluate Themselves? A Probabilistic VC Framework
authors: Jae Oh Woo, Mengdie Flora Wang, Rahul Ghosh, Baishali Chaudhury, Mun Young Kim
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) find increasing use in critical applications, evaluating their ability to assess their own outputs has become crucial. We present a theoretical and empirical framework that examines whether LLMs can differentiate between correct and incorrect solutions while maintaining properly calibrated confidence. Building on classical Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) theory, we adapt it to probabilistic predictors through two complexity metrics: Probabilistic VC (PVC), which measures a model's ability to confidently classify across problem types, and Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC), which additionally demands alignment between confidence scores and actual success rates. Unlike Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Actual Error (AE), these measures give an integrated assessment of self-evaluation expressiveness and calibration, with sample complexity bounds and generalization guarantees comparable to classical VC theory. We test eleven 7-8B models on 360 original mathematical reasoning problems, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA. Each model chooses between two of its own generated solutions and reports its confidence, with ground truth determined by an ensemble of larger models. The results show a systematic inverse relationship: models with greater self-evaluation expressiveness have weaker calibration. s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct achieve the highest PVC-VUS scores, while JiuZhang3.0-7B is best calibrated, with the lowest ECE and the smallest PVC-VUS gap. The trade-off persists across architectures, training paradigms, and domains, pointing to a fundamental challenge in developing self-reflective LLMs, and our framework offers practical tools for diagnosing it.

infographic.key_insight: Across tested LLMs, stronger self-evaluation expressiveness coincided with weaker confidence calibration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Systems that rely on LLM self-assessment should evaluate both correctness discrimination and confidence calibration before trusting model-reported certainty.
method: Extend classical VC theory with Probabilistic VC (PVC) to measure confident classification capacity.
Add Calibration-aware PVC (C-PVC) to require alignment between confidence and actual success rates.
Have models choose between two self-generated solutions and report confidence.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests of eleven 7–8B models on 360 original math problems, TruthfulQA, and CommonsenseQA found s1.1-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct highest in PVC-VUS, while JiuZhang3.0-7B had the lowest ECE.
infographic.watch_item: Ground truth came from an ensemble of larger models, so evaluator errors could affect the measured trade-off.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLMs Reliably Evaluate Themselves? A Probabilistic VC Framework

title: Efficient Detailed Scheduling of Multiproduct Pipelines using Action-Decoupled Deep Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kai Shao, Ling Jian, Liming Liu, Serguey V. Bogomolov, Xinmin Wang
abstract: Multiproduct pipelines transport refined products to delivery stations in sequential batches, and their detailed scheduling must meet market demand while respecting nonlinear hydraulic constraints. Retaining the full hydraulic nonlinearity yields a mixed-integer nonlinear program that is computationally intractable, while the linearization commonly adopted for solver-based optimization degrades hydraulic accuracy without resolving the heavy computational burden. This paper develops an action-decoupled proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that efficiently produces detailed schedules while preserving hydraulic fidelity. The scheduling process is cast as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) with flexible action durations. To handle the discrete-continuous hybrid action space, a cascaded dual-actor architecture decouples the discrete operating duration from the continuous flow decisions, eliminating the gradient interference that destabilizes conventional coupled-action policies and thereby yielding high-quality schedules far more efficiently. Validated on a real-world multiproduct pipeline in China and benchmarked against a single-actor baseline and a linearized MILP solved by Gurobi, the proposed framework achieves delivery accuracy close to the exact optimum while substantially improving flow rate stability and substantially reducing solution time.

infographic.key_insight: Decoupling operating duration from flow decisions enables PPO to generate efficient multiproduct pipeline schedules while preserving nonlinear hydraulic fidelity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets demand-compliant pipeline operations with steadier flow rates and shorter scheduling computation times.
method: Model scheduling as a semi-Markov decision process with flexible action durations.
Use cascaded PPO actors for discrete operating duration and continuous flow decisions.
Decouple action learning to reduce destabilizing gradient interference.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a real-world pipeline in China, comparisons with a single-actor baseline and a Gurobi-solved linearized MILP show reported near-optimal delivery accuracy, improved flow stability, and reduced solution time.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative gains or evidence of generalization beyond the evaluated pipeline.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Detailed Scheduling of Multiproduct Pipelines using Action-Decoupled Deep Reinforcement Learning

title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization
authors: Thien Le, Melanie Weber
abstract: Graph neural networks are often trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones, raising the question of which graph information must be preserved for combinatorial optimization values to transfer across sizes. We establish size-transfer guarantees for normalized graph optimization values using finite collections of energy features. For affine objectives, including MAX-CUT, coloring defect, and independent-set density, differences in task value are controlled by discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes on all bounded-degree graphs. For general Lipschitz objectives, such as those with balance penalties, an additional representation error appears; this error vanishes on hyperfinite graph families but can remain bounded away from zero on expanders. Thus, at fixed degree bound, state space, Lipschitz constant, and target accuracy, a finite energy representation independent of graph size suffices universally for affine tasks and asymptotically for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families. These results yield prediction guarantees under explicit conditions on encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage, together with statistical generalization bounds. Theoretically, we prove Shapley-Folkman bounds with sharp parameter dependence, including a dimension-free $\ell_2$ regime, and realize the resulting energy features with a fixed-weight message-passing network using random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs. Experiments with exact solvers and trained models test the resulting transfer guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: Finite energy features independent of graph size can control normalized optimization values across bounded-degree graphs for affine tasks, with asymptotic guarantees for general Lipschitz tasks on hyperfinite families.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results identify conditions under which graph models trained on small instances can predict optimization values on larger instances.
method: Bound task-value differences using discrepancies in normalized scalar energy probes.
Use Shapley–Folkman bounds to quantify representation error for general Lipschitz objectives.
Realize energy features with fixed-weight message passing and random node initialization on bounded-treewidth graphs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments use exact solvers and trained models to test transfer guarantees; the abstract reports no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: General Lipschitz tasks can retain nonvanishing representation error on expanders, and prediction guarantees require encoder accuracy, readout stability, and representation coverage.
infographic.paper_title: On Sparse Graph Limits for Neural Combinatorial Optimization

title: ParaDeAl: Parallel Descent Algorithms for Sparse Statistics
authors: Adam Deng, Rahul Mazumder
abstract: Best subset selection is a central problem in statistical regression, drawing increasing attention from the broader optimization and machine learning communities. Solving the hard L0 sparsity constraint directly has been computationally challenging; as a result, most existing work proposes formulations which do not enforce the constraint, but instead use a mix of L0/L1/L2 penalties to encourage sparsity. Modern methods for solving such penalized formulations are tractable for p = 100,000, but give up direct control over sparsity. In this paper, we propose a two-stage proximal gradient descent-based approach which both enforces the sparsity constraint and incorporates L1/L2 penalties, leveraging GPUs for computational acceleration to find approximate solutions. Our method, ParaDeAl, offers the user the ability to select the problem hyperparameters, solves all configurations in parallel, and obtains solutions up to 15x faster than the best state-of-the-art CPU competitors while achieving almost identical test accuracy for the same support size for large (p > 100,000) synthetic and real-world datasets.

infographic.key_insight: ParaDeAl combines explicit sparsity constraints with L1/L2 penalties and GPU parallelism to accelerate approximate best subset selection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables direct control over the number of selected regression features while evaluating multiple hyperparameter configurations in parallel.
method: Use a two-stage proximal gradient descent approach.
Enforce an L0 sparsity constraint alongside L1/L2 penalties.
Solve user-selected hyperparameter configurations in parallel on GPUs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports up to 15× speedups over leading CPU competitors on large synthetic and real-world datasets with p > 100,000, with almost identical test accuracy at the same support size.
infographic.watch_item: Solutions are approximate, and the reported GPU-versus-CPU speedup may depend on hardware and workload.
infographic.paper_title: ParaDeAl: Parallel Descent Algorithms for Sparse Statistics

title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model
authors: Avetik Arakelyan, Davit Alaverdyan, Naira Hovakimyan, Isaac Kaminer, Tigran Bakaryan
abstract: In this work we address a class of Mean-Field Game (MFG) systems on the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^{d}$ in which individual agent incentives arise from macroscopic, distribution-dependent objectives governed by the Wasserstein-2 ($W_{2}$) distance. Taking the first variation (Lions derivative) of the Wasserstein-based macroscopic functional yields a coupled forward-backward system of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) and Fokker--Planck (FP) equations featuring a nonlocal coupling driven by the Kantorovich optimal transport potential. As a primary case study, we formulate a large-scale attacker-defender attrition model aimed at protecting High-Value Units (HVUs). By defining population-wise attrition rates via the $W_{2}$ metric and casting the defense strategy as a Pareto-optimal McKean--Vlasov control problem, we derive a concrete HJB--FP system with a Kantorovich potential coupling. We prove the local-in-time existence of classical solutions for this system using Schauder's fixed-point theorem. Finally, we compute the MFG dynamics by combining the Sinkhorn algorithm with ResNet-based Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and simulate two-dimensional attacker-defender engagements across diverse attrition parameters, control costs, and multi-HVU configurations.

infographic.key_insight: Wasserstein-2 population objectives yield mean-field game equations coupled through Kantorovich optimal transport potentials, enabling a model of large-scale attacker–defender attrition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports modeling coordinated defense of high-value units while balancing population attrition and control costs.
method: Derive coupled HJB–Fokker–Planck equations from Wasserstein-based objectives.
Prove local-in-time classical solution existence using Schauder’s fixed-point theorem.
Compute dynamics with Sinkhorn optimal transport and ResNet-based physics-informed neural networks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports two-dimensional engagement simulations varying attrition parameters, control costs, and multiple high-value-unit configurations.
infographic.watch_item: The existence guarantee is local in time, and the abstract does not report numerical error bounds or scalability benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model

title: On a Class of Non-Local Elliptic-Transport Systems in Score-Guided Probability Flow on $SE(3)$: Score-Singularity Resolution, Space-Time ADN Shift, and Markov Mean-Field Games
authors: Pilhwa Lee
abstract: We establish mathematical foundations for optimal spatiotemporal vector fields governing continuous score-guided probability flows over bounded submanifolds $M \subset SE(3)$ on the Special Euclidean group $SE(3) \cong \mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3)$. Modeling dynamic density evolution via a score-perturbed Lie-algebraic continuity equation under zero-flux boundary conditions, we resolve the non-local score drift singularity $s(g,t) = \nabla_{SE(3)} \log ρ(g,t)$ as $ρ\rightarrow 0^+$ via weighted parabolic flux dissipation bounds. Using left-invariant exponential group mollifiers, we derive boundary-preserving DiPerna--Lions commutator estimates tracking structure constants $\{c_{ij}^k\}$. Second, interpreting the optimality system as a 7D space-time elliptic operator $L_{7D} = -Δ_{SE(3)} - \partial_t^2$ with zero-order corner compatibility on $\partial M \times \{0,T\}$, we establish Agmon--Douglis--Nirenberg $W_p^2(Q_T)$ shift estimates tracking Lie algebra constants, boundary geometry $\|\partial M\|_{C^2}$, and Ricci curvature $\|Ric_{SE(3)}\|_{L^\infty}$, yielding a full $C^\infty(\overline{Q}_T)$ Schauder bootstrap expansion. Third, we extend this system to non-cooperative Markov Mean-Field Games (MFGs) on $SE(3)$, establishing score-guided Nash equilibria via Schauder--Tychonoff fixed points. Crucially, the constant diagonal Ricci curvature $Ric_{SE(3)} = \mathrm{diag}(0,0,0,1/2,1/2,1/2)$ from $SO(3)$ induces a sharp Bochner--Weitzenböck spectral gap boost $λ_1(-Δ_{SE(3)}) \ge λ_1(-Δ_{\mathbb{R}^3}) + 1/2 > 0$. This positive rotational curvature enhances the Lie-algebraic Poincaré coercivity constant, demonstrating that intrinsic group curvature stabilizes score-guided flows against dispersion and expands the critical Nash uniqueness horizon $T_{SE(3)}^*$ beyond flat Euclidean limits.

infographic.key_insight: The paper develops a theoretical framework for score-guided probability flows on SE(3), addressing low-density score singularities, space–time regularity, and mean-field game equilibria.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could inform stable generative models and multi-agent control for systems combining 3D position and orientation.
method: Control singular score drift using weighted flux dissipation and boundary-preserving Lie-group mollification.
Apply 7D space–time elliptic estimates to analyze regularity.
Use Schauder–Tychonoff fixed points to establish score-guided Nash equilibria.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical bounds and existence results, but no numerical experiments, datasets, or empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The claimed additive spectral-gap boost requires careful verification of metric, domain, and boundary assumptions; positive rotational Ricci curvature alone does not establish it.
infographic.paper_title: On a Class of Non-Local Elliptic-Transport Systems in Score-Guided Probability Flow on $SE(3)$: Score-Singularity Resolution, Space-Time ADN Shift, and Markov Mean-Field Games
